facts.fact: Ingenito, Lima and Buckup described the species in 2013 in the journal Neotropical Ichthyology.
The species was described from the middle rio Juruena drainage of the upper rio Tapajós basin in Mato Grosso, Brazil.
The holotype is MNRJ 38988, a male collected on 5 May 2006 from a stream at fazenda São Nicolau in Cotriguaçu, Mato Grosso.
The name honours the Peugeot family. Their business funded a carbon-sink reforestation project at fazenda São Nicolau, and that project led to the fish's discovery.
The Peugeot family being honoured is not the carmaker. The video credits them with inventing the pepper-mill mechanism.
Because the name honours a family, the grammatically strict form would be peugeotorum. Some pages use that spelling.
The Catalog of Fishes lists Hyphessobrycon peugeoti as valid and says the epithet does not need correcting.
The Catalog of Fishes places the species in the family Acestrorhamphidae, subfamily Hyphessobryconinae.
In life the fish is carmine red overall. The top of the head and back are dark red, the flanks and belly are silvery with red pigment cells, and the fins are red.
It has a dark blotch on the caudal peduncle.
Its red colour in life separates it from the silvery or golden H. elachys and H. heliacus.
It differs from H. loweae in having five scale rows between the dorsal-fin origin and the lateral line, against 6–7 in H. loweae.
It also differs from H. loweae in having 21–24 branched anal-fin rays, against 17–21.
The description does not assess the species' conservation status.
It is known from tributaries of the middle rio Juruena, in the upper rio Tapajós basin in Mato Grosso, Brazil.
The video says it comes from a remote part of Mato Grosso, in the upper Rio Tapajós and more precisely the Rio Juruena.
It was collected in water less than 1 m deep at the start of the dry season.
The type locality was a swampy, deforested area beside road MT-208, with the water choked by grasses and small shrubs.
One specimen came from a flowing stream with a sandy bottom and clear water.
Other paratypes came from a flooded area next to the rio Juruena.
The video says the species lives in clear water with few aquatic plants, a sandy bottom and plenty of detritus.
The video says it lives in small shallow streams and in swamps created by the destruction of the rainforest.
The video gives a temperature of about 22–26 °C for its wild habitat.
It is in the aquarium trade. Aquarium Glaser offers captive-bred fish to wholesalers.
A UK retailer sells F1 Peugeot tetras.
The retailer advises adding it only to a cycled, mature aquarium.
The video recommends a tank of at least 80 L for a group.
Later in the video the keeper says the tank should be well planted and hold at least 100 L, because the fish need swimming space.
A retailer suggests at least about 45–60 L for a small group.
A retailer gives 24–28 °C, pH 5.5–7.0 and soft to moderately soft water.
The fish show their best colour in dim light. Floating plants are recommended.
Aquarium Glaser found the fish only coloured up after the tank was darkened a lot. Warmer water, humic substances, live food and water changes did not bring the colour back.
In the video it took frozen food, flakes and granules straight away.
The video keeper feeds frozen Artemia, Cyclops and Bosmina, and says live food is preferred and helps with breeding.
It feeds near the surface and rarely goes deep for food. Slow-eating tankmates can go hungry.
A retailer describes it as an omnivore. It suggests micro pellets or fine flakes plus daphnia, baby brine shrimp, cyclops and bloodworm.
It is a schooling fish. The video recommends a group of at least 10–12.
It is peaceful overall, but some males can be territorial.
It suits other small peaceful fish such as dwarf cichlids and other tetras. Adult Neocaridina shrimp were safe with it, but baby shrimp may not survive.
It swims fast and is a poor match for slow eaters.
Aquarium Glaser describes it as completely peaceful.
A retailer says to keep it in groups of at least six to eight, and that mature males may display to one another.
Adult males have a long, filamentous dorsal fin. In fully grown males it reaches the base of the tail when laid flat.
Males have a nearly straight anal-fin margin with thickened rays, and a stronger caudal-peduncle blotch. Females have a normal dorsal fin and a lobed anal fin.
Females are less intensely red and black than males.
Males grow about 20% bigger than females.
Males can show a black tail fin as breeding colour. The tail fin is otherwise transparent.
The video keeper had not bred it in the aquarium yet, but saw males displaying and females following them into the plants.
Based on the keeper's reading, the video says females can lay several hundred eggs on plants or the substrate.
According to the video, eggs hatch in 24–36 hours and the fry swim freely after 3–4 days.
The video advises separating the adults from the eggs and fry.
Captive-bred fish are offered in the trade, so it has been bred in aquaria.

care.quote: It grows about 4 to 5 cm, but usually 4.5.
it should be around 22 to 26° C
